original_question: Replace the circle in the circumscribed-polygon concurrency problem by an ellipse, and consider a polygon all of whose sides are tangent to that ellipse. How many concurrent lines can occur among the polygon's diagonals and the lines connecting the contact points of two non-adjacent sides?
target_in_paper: Open Problem 2.3, i.e. the ellipse analogue of Problem 2’s circumscribed-polygon concurrency question. Its immediate context is Problem 2 together with Open Problem 2.1-2.5. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper very closely: it replaces the circle by an ellipse, keeps the polygon tangent to that curve, and asks about concurrency among the same two families of lines singled out in Open Problem 2.3—polygon diagonals and lines joining tangency points coming from non-adjacent sides. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))
missing_details: The paper inherits from Problem 2 the hypothesis that the polygon has at least 4 sides, so a stand-alone version should state n≥4 explicitly. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))

The ambient setting is Euclidean plane geometry: the ellipse is inside the polygon and every side of the polygon is tangent to it (the author’s informal term is an 'ellipsoscribed' polygon). ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))

The relevant 'contact points' are the tangency points of the sides with the ellipse, and the auxiliary lines are taken for pairs of non-adjacent sides, i.e. sides not sharing a vertex. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))

To make the problem fully stand-alone, one should name the entire line family explicitly: all diagonals of the polygon, plus for each pair of non-adjacent sides the line joining their two tangency points. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))

The phrase 'how many concurrent lines' should be sharpened to mean 'how many lines from this family can pass through one common point'; otherwise the formulation leaves open whether the intended task is an existence question, a maximum question, or a classification of all possible concurrency counts. This is a clarification of the paper’s informal wording. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))

There are no ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or asymptotic quantifier conditions anywhere nearby; the hidden data that matter here are only the Euclidean setting, the side-count parameter n, and the precise definition of the line family. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))
refined_question: In the Euclidean plane, let P be an n-gon with n≥4 whose sides are all tangent to a fixed ellipse E contained in P. Consider the family of lines consisting of every diagonal of P and, for each pair of non-adjacent sides of P, the line joining their tangency points with E. How many lines in this family can be concurrent at a single point? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))
justification: This is the correct target because the draft does not ask for the circle-case conditions for having more than three concurrent lines (Open Problem 2.1) or for the circle-case maximum (Open Problem 2.2). Instead, it directly asks for the ellipse replacement of the circumscribed-polygon concurrency problem, which is exactly what Open Problem 2.3 does. Problem 2 supplies the inherited setup—polygon with at least four sides, diagonals plus tangency-point joins, and the motivating circle result that at least three such lines are concurrent—while the surrounding text shows that the ellipse case is intended as the immediate 2D variant of that same construction, not as a broader conic or higher-dimensional reformulation. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/MultispaceMultistructure.pdf))
